title: IoT and AI Control of Aquaponic Farms
headline: Joint PhD with UWE: an IoT sensing platform ran for 12 months on a commercial aquaponics farm, and AI models used its data to detect anomalies and cut grid heating energy by up to 27%
photoAlt: Inside the aquaponics research greenhouse, with vertical towers, grow beds and plants
subtitle: A joint PhD with UWE: twelve months of IoT data from a commercial aquaponics farm, used to detect faults early and cut heating energy
need: Aquaponics raises fish and grows plants in one recirculating system, using far less water and no soil or pesticides. But its biology, chemistry and physics are tightly linked, and most farms still rely on manual checks and fixed alarm thresholds that miss slow drifts and sensor faults.

Energy is the other barrier. Pumping, aeration and above all water heating make aquaponics expensive to run in a cold climate. Published research had mostly used small rigs, a few sensors and short trials, so there was little long-term data from a real commercial farm to build better control on.
role: SciFlair co-funded the PhD with the University of the West of England and provided the IoT engineering and industrial support. The sensing platform was deployed on a commercial aquaponics farm in the UK.
built: An edge sensing unit measuring nine parameters: water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, plus air temperature, humidity and light
Signal conditioning, wireless communication and cloud storage, with applications to view the data and raise alerts
Local rule-based control in the hardware, validated in the lab and kept disabled on the live farm to protect fish welfare
A twelve-month, high-resolution dataset from a working commercial farm, capturing seasonal change, farm activity and real sensor faults
Anomaly detection compared across statistical, Isolation Forest, neural network, LSTM and GRU models, to catch sensor faults, spikes and gradual drift early
An energy-aware heating controller that uses the water's thermal mass and solar forecasts to heat when solar power is available, within safe limits for fish, plants and bacteria

delivery.title: Concept
delivery.text: A literature review found that most systems use few sensors, short trials and fixed thresholds, and set the research questions on sensing, anomaly detection and energy.

delivery.title: Design and build
delivery.text: Designed the edge sensing unit, probe head and cloud architecture to collect water-quality and climate data reliably on a working farm.

delivery.title: Field operation
delivery.text: Ran the platform continuously for twelve months on a commercial aquaponics farm in the UK, despite sensor noise, farm activity and patchy communications.

delivery.title: Analysis and validation
delivery.text: Evaluated five anomaly-detection methods on the farm data, and simulated the energy-aware heating controller against a standard thermostat using a year of real conditions.

delivery.title: Completion
delivery.text: The thesis was submitted in December 2025 and the researcher graduated in 2026.

nextGen.title: Next: Commercial Aquaponics Control
nextGen.text: The next step is to switch on closed-loop control on a working farm and add the energy-aware heating controller with solar power. We are looking for growers, partners and funders to take it there.
